cards.explanation: The answer is Baal. Jehoram, Ahab's son and king of Israel, removes the sacred pillar of Baal that his father had made (2 Kings 3:2). That's a real step, friends. But the very next verse says he still clung to the sins of Jeroboam. It's like wiping down one counter and leaving flour on every other surface in the kitchen.

The answer is False. The text says he clung to the sins that Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit, and he did not turn away from them (2 Kings 3:3). Clung is a tight grip, friends. So even with the pillar of Baal removed, there's still something he won't let go of.

The answer is that Mesha, king of Moab, rebels against the king of Israel. After Ahab's death, Mesha rebelled (2 Kings 3:5). Ahab was Jehoram's father (2 Kings 3:1), and Jehoram is the king who sets out to deal with it (2 Kings 3:6). I'd call that a rough inheritance.
The answer is True. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, answers Jehoram, king of Israel, “I will go…” (2 Kings 3:7). He doesn't hem and haw or say he'll check his calendar. He just says yes.

The answer is, “By way of the Desert of Edom…” (2 Kings 3:8). The king of Edom joins them too, so there are three kings on this road (2 Kings 3:9). Friends, a desert route sounds like a plan that needs a lot of water. Hold that thought.

The answer is water. After a roundabout route of seven days, the army had no water for their army or for their animals (2 Kings 3:9). Seven days of traveling and no water, friends. That's a very dry army.

The answer is that the LORD has summoned three kings to hand them over to Moab. The king of Israel cries, “Alas… for the LORD has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab!” (2 Kings 3:10). That's the king's own take on the situation, friends. Watch what a prophet of the LORD says about it next.

The answer is prophet. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, asks, “Is there no prophet of the LORD here? Let us inquire of the LORD through him.” (2 Kings 3:11). He wants to hear from the LORD, not just fret. That's a good thing to ask when the canteens are empty.

The answer is True. Jehoshaphat says, “The word of the LORD is with him.” (2 Kings 3:12). He's talking about Elisha son of Shaphat, the man a servant of the king of Israel named, who used to pour water on the hands of Elijah. After hearing that, the three kings go down to see him.

The answer is that Elisha tells the king of Israel to go to the prophets of his parents. Elisha says, “What have we to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and of your mother!” (2 Kings 3:13). That's not a warm hello, friends. The king answers, “No, … for it is the LORD who has summoned these three kings to deliver them into the hand of Moab.” (2 Kings 3:13).

The answer is his regard for Jehoshaphat king of Judah. Elisha says, “As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, were it not for my regard for the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or acknowledge you.” (2 Kings 3:14). So Jehoshaphat's presence is the reason Elisha names. I'd want Jehoshaphat around too.

The answer is the hand of the LORD. While the harpist played, “…the hand of the LORD came upon Elisha” (2 Kings 3:15). Then he speaks the LORD's word to the three kings. I'm no prophet, friends, but a little harp music sounds like a good start.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “You will not see wind or rain, but the valley will be filled with water, and you will drink…” (2 Kings 3:17). He says the cattle and the animals will drink too. No wind and no rain, friends, and the valley still fills.

The answer is simple. Elisha says, “This is a simple matter in the sight of the LORD, and He will also deliver the Moabites into your hand.” (2 Kings 3:18). Filling a dry valley and handing over an enemy is a simple matter for Him. For me, friends, it's hard enough to get a batch out of the oven on time.

The answer is the next morning at the morning sacrifice. The next morning, at the time of the morning sacrifice, water suddenly flowed from the direction of Edom and filled the land (2 Kings 3:20). Suddenly is the word, friends. There's no long wait after the LORD speaks.

The answer is as red as blood. The sun was shining on the water, and it looked as red as blood to the Moabites across the way (2 Kings 3:22). The text tells us how it looked to them, with the sun shining on it. That's the whole picture they had, friends.

The answer is True. The Moabites exclaim, “This is blood! The kings have clashed swords and slaughtered one another. Now to the plunder, Moab!” (2 Kings 3:23). They saw red water and made up the whole story from it. I think that's a big conclusion to jump to from one look across the way.

The answer is False. When the Moabites came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and attacked them, and they fled before them (2 Kings 3:24). The camp wasn't empty, friends, because the Israelites rose up. That's a hard welcome for anybody.

The answer is spring and tree. Elisha's word included, “…stop up every spring…” (2 Kings 3:19), and the text says the Israelites “…stopped up every spring…” (2 Kings 3:25). Elisha also said they would “…cut down every good tree…” (2 Kings 3:19), and the text says the Israelites did (2 Kings 3:25). Spring and tree are the pair, friends.

The answer is False. The king of Moab took seven hundred swordsmen to break through to the king of Edom, “…but they could not prevail.” (2 Kings 3:26). Seven hundred swordsmen is a lot of men, friends. It still wasn't enough.

The answer is that the Israelites withdraw and return to their own land. There was great fury against the Israelites, “…so they withdrew and returned to their own land.” (2 Kings 3:27). It's a heavy ending to a heavy scene, friends. The text doesn't say more about the fury than that.
